questions.q: What are the three phases of the attack continuum across which an organization needs visibility and control?

choices.why: These are incident response activities, not the three phases of the attack continuum, which are before, during, and after.
These are security functions, not the continuum phases. The continuum phases are before, during, and after an attack.

choices.text: Before, during, and after an attack
choices.why: Correct. The attack continuum covers before an attack, during an active attack, and after the attacker starts to damage systems or steal information.
These are attacker kill-chain style stages; the attack continuum is defined simply as before, during, and after an attack.

questions.q: Which organization's definition of EDR does the chapter cite, describing it as tools primarily focused on detecting and investigating suspicious activities on hosts and endpoints?

choices.why: Correct. The chapter uses Gartner's definition of Endpoint Detection and Response.
NIST publishes security frameworks, but the chapter credits the EDR definition to Gartner.
MITRE is known for ATT&CK, but the chapter's EDR definition comes from Gartner.
Talos is Cisco's threat intelligence group that works with the Malware Analytics Cloud; it is not the source of the EDR definition.

questions.q: Which term describes the problem where an EDR produces so many false positives that real threats are more likely to go unnoticed?

choices.why: Threat blocking is an EDR capability that contains threats rather than just detecting them; it does not describe excess false positives.
Retrospection, or cloud recall, is going back to quarantine a file once it is later found to be bad, not a false-positive problem.
Correct. Alert fatigue is caused by too many false positives, and good EDR filtering exists to reduce it.
Device flow correlation flags or blocks suspicious network activity; it is a feature, not a symptom of too many false positives.

questions.q: How does the Cisco Secure Endpoint connector decide whether a file is malicious, compared with traditional antivirus?

choices.text: It sends the file's hash to the cloud, and the cloud returns a verdict
choices.why: Correct. Instead of matching a local signature database, the lightweight connector sends a hash to the cloud, which decides.

choices.text: It compares the file name against an allowed-application list
choices.why: Secure Endpoint identifies files by SHA-256 hash, not by name, and the verdict comes from the cloud.

choices.text: It uploads every file to a local sandbox appliance
choices.why: The connector does not sandbox every file locally; it sends hashes to the Malware Analytics Cloud for a verdict.

choices.text: It matches the file against a large local signature database
choices.why: That is how traditional antivirus works. Secure Endpoint offloads the decision to the cloud so the connector stays lightweight.

questions.q: Which three verdicts can the Malware Analytics Cloud return to a Secure Endpoint connector?

choices.why: Correct. Figure 11-1 shows the cloud returning Clean, Malware, or Unknown.
These are actions a policy might take, not the verdicts the cloud returns, which are Clean, Malware, and Unknown.
These are not the Secure Endpoint verdicts. The cloud returns Clean, Malware, or Unknown.
These are generic reputation labels; the Secure Endpoint cloud verdicts are Clean, Malware, and Unknown.

questions.q: A security analyst wants to know which endpoints in the organization have seen a particular file. Which Secure Endpoint capability provides this?

choices.why: File sandboxing runs unknown files to see their true behavior, not to track which endpoints have seen them.
File reputation analyzes files inline to block them or apply policies; it does not map where a file has been seen.
Correct. File trajectory shows which endpoints have seen a file.
Device trajectory shows what actions files performed on one given endpoint, not which endpoints saw a file.

questions.q: Which of the following lists the four categories found under the Outbreak Control menu in the Secure Endpoint console?

choices.text: Custom Detections, Exclusions, Engines, and Groups
choices.why: Exclusions and groups are managed under Management, and engines are policy settings; they are not Outbreak Control categories.

choices.text: Policies, Groups, Exclusions, and Download Connector
choices.why: These are items under the Management menu, not the Outbreak Control categories.
These are reporting views in the console, not Outbreak Control categories.

choices.text: Custom Detections, Application Control, Network, and Endpoint IOC
choices.why: Correct. These four categories make up Outbreak Control, and their objects become parts of policies.

questions.q: What does a simple custom detection in Cisco Secure Endpoint consist of?

choices.text: A list of directories and file extensions
choices.why: Directories and file extensions are exclusion set entries, which the connector will not scan.

choices.text: A list of SHA-256 file hashes
choices.why: Correct. A simple custom detection is a list of SHA-256 hashes for files to detect and quarantine.

choices.text: A list of IPv4 addresses in CIDR notation
choices.why: IPv4 addresses in CIDR notation are entries in IP allow and block lists used by DFC, not simple custom detections.
ClamAV-based signatures are used by advanced custom detections, not simple ones.

questions.q: On which antivirus signature format are Secure Endpoint advanced custom detections based?

choices.why: YARA is a separate pattern-matching rule format; the chapter says advanced custom detections are based on ClamAV signatures.
Correct. Advanced custom detections support more signature types, like traditional antivirus signatures, and are based on ClamAV.
Snort is an intrusion prevention rule language, not the basis for Secure Endpoint advanced custom detections.
TETRA is the full client-side antivirus engine in Secure Endpoint, not the signature format for advanced custom detections.

questions.q: An administrator wants connectors to flag or block network connections to known malicious IP addresses, using both the Cisco intelligence feed and the company's own IP lists. Which feature does this?

choices.why: Exclusion sets tell the connector what not to scan or convict; they do not block network connections.
Correct. DFC flags or blocks suspicious network activity and can use the Cisco intelligence feed, your own IP lists, or both.
Advanced custom detections match files using ClamAV-based signatures, not network connections to IP addresses.
File retrospection keeps analyzing files as threat levels change; it does not inspect network connections.

questions.q: Which address format is accepted in Secure Endpoint IP allow and block lists?

choices.why: IP lists hold IPv4 addresses or CIDR ranges, not domain names.
IP lists are used by DFC to judge network connections by IPv4 address, not by MAC address.

choices.text: IPv4 addresses, as single IPs or in CIDR notation
choices.why: Correct. Each line holds a single IPv4 address or a CIDR range.
The IP lists take IPv4 addresses only, not IPv6.

questions.q: An engineer finds that the Secure Endpoint connector slows down a database server because it scans large, frequently written files. What should the engineer configure?

choices.text: An exclusion set for the database directory
choices.why: Correct. Exclusion sets fix performance problems by excluding directories with large, frequently written files like databases.
Enabling TETRA makes the connector a thicker client using more disk and bandwidth, which would not help performance.

choices.text: A simple custom detection for the database files
choices.why: A simple custom detection would detect and quarantine the files by hash, which is the opposite of what is needed.

choices.text: An IP allow list for the database server
choices.why: An IP allow list stops DFC from blocking or flagging addresses; it does not stop file scanning.

questions.q: Which Secure Endpoint engine is a full client-side antivirus engine that is disabled by default?

choices.why: Ethos is the fuzzy fingerprinting engine using static or passive heuristics, not a full antivirus engine.
ClamAV is the signature format behind advanced custom detections, not one of the three Secure Endpoint engines.
Spero is the machine learning engine that finds previously unknown threats, not a full client-side antivirus.
Correct. TETRA is the full client-side antivirus engine, and the default is to leave it disabled.

questions.q: By default, which port do Secure Endpoint connectors use to reach the Cisco cloud servers for file and network disposition lookups?

choices.why: The lookups use TCP 443 (HTTPS), not UDP.
Correct. Connectors use HTTPS on TCP 443 by default, so firewalls and web proxies must allow it.
UDP 53 is DNS, which connectors need to resolve the cloud server names, but it is not the lookup port.
TCP 32137 is the alternative port; the default is TCP 443.

questions.q: What is the maximum size of a file you can upload to the Secure Endpoint console so the cloud can calculate its SHA-256 hash for a custom detection?

choices.why: The upload limit is 20MB; there is no 1GB upload option for hashing.
The upload limit for hashing is 20MB, well below 100MB.
The limit is 20MB, not 2MB.
Correct. Files up to 20MB can be uploaded so the system extracts the SHA-256.

questions.q: Which Secure Endpoint console view shows threat activity in the organization over the past 30 days along with the percentage of compromised computers?

choices.why: iOS Clarity shows activity for iOS devices managed through a linked MDM, not the overall 30-day threat summary.
Correct. The Main Dashboard shows the past 30 days of threat activity and the percentage of compromised computers.
The Events dashboard lists the most recent events in the deployment rather than a 30-day summary.
The audit log is the change history for lists and exclusion sets, not a threat activity view.

questions.q: An engineer wants to give Cisco Secure Client users the Secure Endpoint connector without a separate installer process. Which component helps distribute it?

choices.why: Correct. The AMP Enabler is a Cisco Secure Client add-on that helps distribute the Secure Endpoint connector to Cisco Secure Client users.
Cisco Threat Response is a one-pane-of-glass console that integrates security products; it does not install connectors.
iOS Clarity is a dashboard for MDM-managed iOS devices; it does not distribute connectors.
DFC flags or blocks suspicious network activity; it has nothing to do with distributing the connector.

questions.q: In the Secure Endpoint console, how is a policy applied to endpoints?

choices.why: Exclusion sets are parts of a policy, not the means of applying the policy to endpoints.
IP block lists are DFC objects included in policies; they do not assign policies to endpoints.
The Inbox tracks compromised computers; it is not used to assign policies.
Correct. A policy reaches endpoints through groups, which organize computers by function, location, or other criteria.

questions.q: A company wants mobile devices kept on a supported set of applications, with automated patch provisioning and jailbreak detection. Which type of solution meets this need?

choices.why: File retrospection continues analyzing files as threat levels change; it does not manage devices.
DFC flags or blocks suspicious network connections; it does not manage device configuration or patching.
EDR focuses on detecting and investigating suspicious activity on endpoints, not on provisioning patches or enforcing an app catalog.
Correct. MDM keeps devices on supported apps and corporate policies, provisions updates and patches automatically, and monitors jailbreak detection.

questions.q: Which Cisco product is described as an ongoing effort toward one console that automates integrations across Cisco security products such as Secure Endpoint, Umbrella, and Secure Email?

choices.why: Meraki SM is Cisco's MDM, which feeds iOS Clarity; it is not the cross-product security console.
The Email Security Appliance processes email through listeners; it is one of the products integrated, not the integrating console.
Correct. Cisco Threat Response is the one-pane-of-glass console integrating Cisco security products and threat intelligence sources.
Cisco Secure Client provides remote access VPN, secure network access, and ISE posture; it is not the integration console.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Cisco Secure Endpoint?

choices.why: File retrospection, continuing to analyze files as threat levels change, is a Secure Endpoint feature.
Device trajectory, showing what files did on a given endpoint, is a Secure Endpoint feature.
Correct. Web content filtering and redirect is not a Secure Endpoint feature; the chapter quiz makes this point.
Custom detections, under Outbreak Control, are a core Secure Endpoint feature for detecting and quarantining files.

questions.q: What does EPP (Endpoint Protection Platform) add beyond basic detection?

choices.why: Automated patch provisioning is an MDM function, not what defines EPP.
Remote access VPN is provided by Cisco Secure Client, not by the EPP concept.
Listeners belong to the Cisco ESA and handle incoming SMTP connections; they are unrelated to EPP.
Correct. EPP provides detection plus protection, meaning it blocks threats.

questions.q: What does Cisco call the software agent installed on an endpoint for Secure Endpoint monitoring and detection?

choices.why: Correct. Cisco calls the lightweight Secure Endpoint agent a connector.
Sensor is a generic term; Cisco specifically calls the Secure Endpoint agent a connector.
A listener is an ESA component that handles incoming SMTP connections, not the endpoint agent.
The AMP Enabler is a Cisco Secure Client add-on that distributes the connector; it is not the agent itself.

questions.q: Which minimum EDR capability is about removing false positives so analysts are not overwhelmed?

choices.why: Correct. Filtering removes false positives to reduce alert fatigue.
Threat blocking means containing threats, not just detecting them; it does not address false positives.
Retrospection quarantines files later found to be bad; it is not one of the three minimum EDR capabilities.
DFIR help supports forensics, incident response, and threat hunting rather than reducing false positives.

questions.q: A file passed through several endpoints and was judged clean. A week later, the cloud learns the file is malicious, and the connectors that already saw it go back and quarantine it. What is this called?

choices.why: File reputation analyzes files inline at the time they are seen; going back afterward is retrospection.
Correct. Retrospective security, or cloud recall, quarantines files already seen once they are later found to be bad.
DFC flags or blocks suspicious network connections, not previously seen files.
File sandboxing runs unknown files to observe their behavior; it does not go back to quarantine files already seen.

questions.q: Which Malware Defense feature analyzes unknown files to see their true behavior, matching the dynamic file analysis named in the exam objectives?

choices.why: File reputation analyzes files inline to block them or apply policies, not by running them to observe behavior.
Correct. File sandboxing analyzes unknown files to see their true behavior, which is dynamic file analysis.
File trajectory shows which endpoints have seen a file; it does not analyze behavior.
Ethos is a fuzzy fingerprinting engine using static or passive heuristics, which is the opposite of dynamic analysis.

questions.q: Cisco Secure Endpoint was formerly known by which name?

choices.why: Threat Grid was the former name of Cisco Secure Malware Analytics, the separate sandboxing product.
Correct. Secure Endpoint was formerly Cisco Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) for Endpoints, and before that FireAMP from SourceFire.
AMP for Networks is the former name of Cisco Secure Firewall Malware Defense, the firewall form covered in Chapter 7.
AnyConnect is the former name of Cisco Secure Client, the VPN and posture client.

questions.q: Which hash algorithm does the Secure Endpoint connector send to the cloud, and on which custom detections and application lists are built?

choices.why: Correct. Secure Endpoint identifies files by SHA-256 hash, and detections and lists are built on it.
SHA-1 is not the hash Secure Endpoint uses; it identifies files by SHA-256.
CRC32 is a checksum, not a file identifier used by Secure Endpoint, which uses SHA-256.
MD5 signatures are one type available in advanced custom detections, but the connector's file identifier is SHA-256.

questions.q: In the Secure Endpoint console, a custom detection behaves most like which kind of list?

choices.text: A whitelist of files that must never be scanned
choices.why: Files that must not be scanned belong in an exclusion set, not a custom detection.

choices.text: A list of IP addresses DFC must never block
choices.why: That describes an IP allow list (whitelist) used by DFC, not a custom detection.

choices.text: A blacklist of files to detect and quarantine
choices.why: Correct. A custom detection works like a blacklist, identifying files to detect and quarantine.

choices.text: A list of groups that receive a policy
choices.why: Groups are how policies reach endpoints; they are not custom detections.

questions.q: Which signature types can be used in a Secure Endpoint advanced custom detection?

choices.why: Threat, extension, and path are exclusion types, not signature types.

choices.text: File body-based, MD5, and logical signatures
choices.why: Correct. The chapter quiz lists file body-based signatures, MD5 signatures, and logical signatures as advanced detection types.
Spero, Ethos, and TETRA are Secure Endpoint engines, not signature types for advanced custom detections.
IPv4 addresses, CIDR ranges, and ports are entries in DFC IP lists, not advanced detection signatures.

questions.q: An administrator built an advanced custom detection and added several signatures. Which button must be clicked to compile the signatures into a usable detection?

choices.why: Correct. This button compiles the advanced custom detection, and a success message confirms the signature set was created.
View Changes opens the audit log for a list; it does not build the signature database.
Create IP List starts or finishes a DFC IP list, not an advanced custom detection.
Update Name names a new simple custom detection or renames a list; it does not compile signatures.

questions.q: When an Android custom detection is used for outbreak control and a device has the malicious app installed, what happens?

choices.text: The device is wiped by the connector
choices.why: The connector does not wipe the device; the user is prompted to uninstall the app.

choices.text: The app is silently deleted without notifying the user
choices.why: The chapter says the user is notified and prompted to uninstall; there is no silent deletion.

choices.text: The user is notified and prompted to uninstall the app
choices.why: Correct. For outbreak control, the user is notified and prompted to uninstall the malicious app.

choices.text: The app's network traffic is sent to DFC for blocking
choices.why: DFC deals with network connections by IP address; Android custom detections prompt the user to uninstall the app.

questions.q: What happens to IPv4 addresses that are placed on a Secure Endpoint IP allow list (whitelist)?

choices.text: The connector skips file scanning on hosts with those addresses
choices.why: Skipping scanning is the job of exclusion sets; IP allow lists only affect DFC network decisions.

choices.text: DFC creates detections for connections to them
choices.why: Creating DFC detections is what the IP block list (blacklist) does, not the allow list.

choices.text: They are sent to the cloud for sandboxing
choices.why: IP addresses are not sandboxed; sandboxing analyzes unknown files.

choices.text: DFC never blocks or flags them, ignoring the intelligence feeds for those addresses
choices.why: Correct. The IP allow list holds addresses DFC must never block or flag, and Secure Endpoint ignores the feeds for them.

questions.q: Which navigation path in the Secure Endpoint console is used to create IP allow and block lists?

choices.why: Management > Exclusions lists and creates exclusion sets, not IP lists.

choices.text: Outbreak Control > Application Control > Blocked Applications
choices.why: This path creates application blocking lists by SHA-256, not IP lists.
Management > Policies creates policies that use IP lists, but the lists themselves are created under Outbreak Control > Network.

choices.text: Outbreak Control > Network > IP Block & Allow Lists
choices.why: Correct. IP allow and block lists are created from Outbreak Control > Network > IP Block & Allow Lists.

questions.q: Which four exclusion types can be used in a Secure Endpoint exclusion set?

choices.why: TETRA, Spero, and Ethos are engines and ClamAV is a signature format; none are exclusion types.
These are kinds of custom detections and DFC lists, not exclusion types.
Correct. Exclusion sets support threat, extension, wildcard, and path exclusions.
Clean, Malware, and Unknown are cloud verdicts, not exclusion types.

questions.q: Which statement is true about Cisco-maintained exclusions in Secure Endpoint?

choices.text: They replace the need for custom detections
choices.why: Exclusions say what not to scan; custom detections say what to quarantine. One does not replace the other.

choices.text: They apply only to Android connectors
choices.why: Exclusion sets are created for Windows, Mac, or Linux; Cisco-maintained sets are not Android-only.

choices.text: You must manually update them for each new application version
choices.why: Cisco updates them and adds new ones for new application versions; administrators do not maintain them.

choices.text: You can view them, but you cannot delete or modify them
choices.why: Correct. Cisco creates and updates these exclusion sets for compatibility, and administrators can only view them.

questions.q: Which Secure Endpoint engine is a machine learning technology that uses active heuristics and generic models to proactively find previously unknown threats?

choices.why: Correct. Spero gathers execution attributes with active heuristics and builds generic models to judge software by its general appearance.
Ethos is a fuzzy fingerprinting engine that uses static or passive heuristics, not machine learning on execution attributes.
Talos is Cisco's threat intelligence group, not a Secure Endpoint engine.
TETRA is the full client-side antivirus engine, which relies on signatures rather than machine learning.

questions.q: Besides TCP 443, which alternative port can Secure Endpoint connectors use to reach the Cisco cloud for disposition lookups?

choices.why: TCP 25 is SMTP, which an ESA listener accepts; it is not used for connector cloud lookups.
The alternative port is TCP 32137, not UDP.
TCP 8443 is not the documented alternative; the chapter gives TCP 32137.
Correct. The quiz answer is TCP port 443 or TCP port 32137.

questions.q: In the Secure Endpoint Inbox, which three tabs are used to track compromised computers?

choices.why: These are cloud verdicts, not Inbox tabs.
These are custom detection types, not Inbox tabs.

choices.text: Requires attention, in progress, and resolved
choices.why: Correct. The Inbox has requires attention, in progress, and resolved tabs.
These are operating system tabs used to filter exclusion sets, not Inbox tabs.

questions.q: After a security team links Cisco Meraki SM to Secure Endpoint, which dashboard shows the most recently seen apps on managed iOS devices?

choices.why: The Main Dashboard shows 30 days of threat activity and the percentage of compromised computers, not iOS app inventory.
Correct. Once Meraki SM or another MDM is linked, iOS Clarity shows activity, recently seen apps, and devices that have not reported.
The Inbox tracks compromised computers needing manual work, not iOS apps from an MDM.
The Overview dashboard shows overall environment status with recent threats, not MDM-fed iOS app data.

questions.q: Which industry term does the chapter give as an alternative name for EDR?

choices.why: DFIR is the practice of investigating and responding to incidents, which a good EDR helps with; it is not another name for EDR.
MDM centrally configures, updates, and monitors devices; it is not another term for EDR.
DFC is a Secure Endpoint feature that flags or blocks suspicious network activity, not a synonym for EDR.
Correct. The book gives ETDR alongside EDR and treats them as the same idea.

questions.q: Besides detection and investigation, what does an EDR solution do with endpoint and network events?

choices.text: Converts them into exclusion sets automatically
choices.why: Exclusion sets are created by administrators to stop scanning of certain items; events are not turned into exclusions.

choices.text: Discards them after a local signature match
choices.why: EDR keeps events centrally for investigation; discarding them would defeat its purpose.

choices.text: Records them in a central database for analysis and reporting
choices.why: Correct. EDR records endpoint and network events in a central database for analysis, detection, investigation, and reporting.

choices.text: Forwards them to an ESA listener over SMTP
choices.why: ESA listeners accept incoming SMTP connections for email; they do not collect EDR events.

questions.q: Which minimum EDR capability requires that the solution contain threats rather than only detect them?

choices.why: DFIR help supports forensics, incident response, and threat hunting after the fact; containment is threat blocking.
Correct. Threat blocking means the EDR must contain threats, not just detect them.
Filtering removes false positives to reduce alert fatigue; it does not contain threats.
File trajectory shows which endpoints saw a file; it is a visibility feature, not an EDR minimum capability.

questions.q: An incident responder is investigating one compromised laptop and needs to see what actions files performed on that specific endpoint. Which Secure Endpoint capability should be used?

choices.why: Outbreak Control is the menu for building detection, application, and network lists, not an investigation view of one endpoint.
File trajectory shows which endpoints have seen a file, not what happened on one endpoint.
Correct. Device trajectory shows what actions files performed on a given endpoint.
Cisco-maintained exclusions are compatibility exclusion sets; they show nothing about file activity.

questions.q: Which Malware Defense feature analyzes files inline so they can be blocked or have policies applied?

choices.why: Correct. File reputation analyzes files inline and blocks them or applies policies.
File retrospection keeps analyzing files over time as threat levels change, rather than at the inline decision point.
File sandboxing runs unknown files to see their true behavior; it is not the inline reputation check.
Device trajectory shows what files did on an endpoint; it does not block files inline.

questions.q: In the Secure Endpoint architecture, which component does most of the processing, keeps a historical view of malware activity, and returns verdicts?

choices.why: Correct. The Malware Analytics Cloud does most of the processing, keeps a historical view of malware activity, and returns verdicts.
The connector is deliberately lightweight and sends hashes to the cloud; it does not do most of the processing.
Meraki SM is an MDM that feeds iOS Clarity; it does not process malware verdicts.
Cisco Secure Client provides VPN, network access, and ISE posture; it is not where malware verdicts are made.

questions.q: An administrator wants a Windows path exclusion that works no matter where a common folder lives on each machine. What can be used in the path?

choices.why: Correct. Windows path exclusions can use CSIDL (constant special ID list) names, which are Microsoft names for common file paths.
Logical signatures are used in advanced custom detections, not in path exclusions.
CIDR notation is used for IP list entries, not file paths.
SHA-256 hashes identify files in detections and lists; they are not path variables.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a Secure Endpoint IP block list (blacklist)?

choices.text: To block applications by their SHA-256 hash
choices.why: Blocking applications by hash is application control, not an IP block list.

choices.text: To stop DFC from ever flagging listed addresses
choices.why: That is the IP allow list (whitelist), which DFC must never block or flag.

choices.text: To create DFC detections for connections to listed IPv4 addresses
choices.why: Correct. IP block list addresses are used to create DFC detections, and matches are flagged or blocked as the DFC rule says.

choices.text: To exclude listed hosts from file scanning
choices.why: Exclusion sets control scanning; IP block lists drive DFC network detections.

questions.q: When creating a Secure Endpoint IP list, what can be specified in addition to IPv4 addresses?

choices.why: Web content filtering and redirect is not a Secure Endpoint feature, and IP lists do not take domain names.

choices.text: Port numbers to block or allow
choices.why: Correct. You can also specify port numbers to block or allow in an IP list.
Threat names are used in threat-type exclusions within exclusion sets, not in IP lists.
IP allow and block lists take IPv4 addresses only.

questions.q: An administrator needs to change the entries in an existing Secure Endpoint IP list. Which button retrieves the list's file so it can be changed?

choices.why: Remove deletes an unwanted SHA-256 from a simple detection list; it does not retrieve an IP list file.
Correct. Download gets the IP list's file so you can change it.
On an IP list, Edit only changes the name, not the addresses.
Files included shows the hashes and notes in a simple custom detection, not IP list contents.

questions.q: An administrator creating a new application blocking list types a name but tries to add a hash right away and cannot. What must be done first?

choices.text: Click Build Database From Signature Set
choices.why: That button compiles an advanced custom detection, not an application blocking list.

choices.text: Download the connector for the group
choices.why: Downloading the connector distributes installers; it is not needed to add hashes to a list.

choices.text: Click Save to store the named list
choices.why: Correct. You name the list and click Save; you cannot add applications before saving.

choices.text: Enable the TETRA engine in the policy
choices.why: TETRA is a client-side antivirus engine and is unrelated to creating application blocking lists.

questions.q: How can an administrator build an Android custom detection in the Secure Endpoint console?

choices.text: Add the app's IP address to an IP block list
choices.why: IP block lists drive DFC network detections; they do not identify Android apps.

choices.text: Create a wildcard exclusion for the app
choices.why: Exclusions stop scanning; they would not detect an Android app.

choices.text: Enter the app's name in a ClamAV logical signature
choices.why: Advanced ClamAV-based detections are for Windows and Mac files; Android detections use the .apk or the inventory.

choices.text: Upload the app's .apk file or pick it from the console's inventory list
choices.why: Correct. Android custom detections are built by uploading the .apk or choosing the app from the inventory list.

questions.q: An engineer is deploying Secure Endpoint on servers that also run another vendor's antivirus product. Which exclusion is recommended?

choices.text: Exclude the Secure Endpoint connector's SHA-256
choices.why: Exclusions work by threat, extension, wildcard, or path, and the recommendation targets the other antivirus product, not the connector.
Excluding all executables would disable most protection; the recommendation is to exclude the other product's install location.

choices.text: Exclude the Windows system directory with CSIDL
choices.why: Excluding the whole system directory is not the recommended fix; exclude the other antivirus product's install location.

choices.text: Exclude the other antivirus product's install location
choices.why: Correct. If another antivirus product runs on the computer, the chapter says to exclude its install location.

questions.q: A file sits in a directory covered by an exclusion set, and its SHA-256 is also on a simple custom detection. What happens?

choices.text: The file is sent to file sandboxing instead
choices.why: An excluded file is not scanned or convicted; it is not redirected to sandboxing.

choices.text: DFC blocks the file's network connections
choices.why: DFC works on network connections by IP address and is unrelated to whether an excluded file is checked.

choices.text: The file is not checked, so the custom detection does not act on it
choices.why: Correct. Files in an excluded location are not checked by application blocking, simple custom detections, or advanced custom detections.

choices.text: The custom detection overrides the exclusion and quarantines it
choices.why: The chapter says excluded files are not checked by custom detections, so there is no override.

questions.q: Why does the chapter advise against enabling TETRA when another antivirus product is installed?

choices.text: It disables the Spero and Ethos engines
choices.why: The chapter does not say TETRA disables Spero or Ethos; the concern is the heavier client.

choices.text: It turns the lightweight connector into a thicker client using more disk and bandwidth
choices.why: Correct. TETRA adds local signatures and signature updates, so it uses more disk and bandwidth, which conflicts with another antivirus.

choices.text: It stops the connector from contacting the cloud
choices.why: TETRA does not stop cloud lookups; it adds a local antivirus engine with its own signatures.
Enabling TETRA does not remove Cisco-maintained exclusions; enabling it shows a subsection for file scanning options.

questions.q: Which Secure Endpoint engine is a fuzzy fingerprinting engine that uses static or passive heuristics?

choices.why: Spero is the machine learning engine that uses active heuristics to gather execution attributes.
ClamAV is the signature basis for advanced custom detections, not one of the three engines.
TETRA is the full client-side antivirus engine, not a fuzzy fingerprinting engine.
Correct. Ethos is the fuzzy fingerprinting engine that uses static or passive heuristics.

questions.q: From which Secure Endpoint dashboard can you click a section heading to jump to the related console page to investigate and fix an issue?

choices.why: Correct. On the Overview dashboard, clicking a section heading jumps to the related console page.
The audit log shows change history for lists and exclusion sets; it is not a dashboard.
iOS Clarity shows MDM-managed iOS device activity and apps; the click-through headings belong to the Overview dashboard.
The Events dashboard lists the most recent events in the deployment rather than linked section headings.

questions.q: An analyst marks a compromised computer as resolved in the Secure Endpoint Inbox. What is the result?

choices.text: The computer is moved into a Cisco-maintained exclusion set
choices.why: Resolving a compromise does not change exclusions; it just removes the computer from Dashboard and Inbox data.

choices.text: The computer no longer shows in the Dashboard or Inbox data
choices.why: Correct. A computer marked resolved no longer appears in the Dashboard or Inbox data.

choices.text: The computer is added to an IP allow list
choices.why: IP allow lists are DFC objects created under Outbreak Control; resolving a computer does not add it.
Resolving is a tracking action; it does not uninstall the connector.

questions.q: What is Cisco Secure Client used for, according to the chapter's vocabulary?

choices.text: Handling incoming SMTP connections on an appliance interface
choices.why: That is an ESA listener, not Cisco Secure Client.

choices.text: Managing iOS devices for the iOS Clarity dashboard
choices.why: That is an MDM such as Cisco Meraki SM, not Cisco Secure Client.

choices.text: Returning Clean, Malware, or Unknown verdicts
choices.why: Verdicts come from the Malware Analytics Cloud, not Cisco Secure Client.

choices.text: Remote access VPN, secure network access, and posture assessment with Cisco ISE
choices.why: Correct. Cisco Secure Client provides remote access VPN, secure network access, and ISE posture assessment.

questions.q: A new Secure Endpoint deployment shows connectors unable to get file dispositions. The network has a perimeter firewall and an explicit web proxy. What is the most likely fix?

choices.text: Allow connector traffic to the Cisco cloud on TCP 443 or TCP 32137 through the firewall and proxy
choices.why: Correct. Connectors must reach the cloud through firewalls and web proxies, using TCP 443 by default or TCP 32137.

choices.text: Open UDP 1812 to the Cisco cloud
choices.why: UDP 1812 is RADIUS authentication and is unrelated to Secure Endpoint cloud lookups.

choices.text: Enable TETRA so connectors stop needing the cloud
choices.why: TETRA adds a local antivirus engine but is disabled by default and not the fix; cloud reachability is needed for dispositions.

choices.text: Add the cloud servers to an exclusion set
choices.why: Exclusion sets affect file scanning, not whether connectors can reach the cloud through the network.

questions.q: What does the acronym DFIR stand for in the context of EDR capabilities?

choices.why: Dynamic file analysis and retrospection are Malware Defense features, but DFIR means digital forensics and incident response.
This is not a real expansion; the similar-sounding DFC is device flow correlation, which flags or blocks suspicious network activity.
Correct. DFIR is investigating and responding to incidents, and a good EDR helps with DFIR and threat hunting.
Filtering is a separate EDR capability; DFIR stands for digital forensics and incident response.

questions.q: Which statement about how EDR solutions differ from one another is accurate according to the chapter?

choices.text: EDR solutions never use an endpoint agent
choices.why: The chapter says an agent on the endpoint typically does ongoing monitoring and detection.

choices.text: Some do more analysis on the agent, while others do more on the back end
choices.why: Correct. Not all EDR solutions work the same; some analyze more on the agent and others in a back-end management console.

choices.text: EDR solutions only operate after an attack has finished
choices.why: EDR provides visibility across the attack continuum, including before and during an attack.

choices.text: All EDR solutions rely only on a local signature database
choices.why: Modern EDR solutions take in threat intelligence from the cloud, and Secure Endpoint sends hashes to the cloud rather than relying on local signatures.

questions.q: Which three components make up the Cisco Secure Malware Defense architecture described in the chapter?

choices.text: The Malware Analytics Cloud, client connectors, and intelligence sources
choices.why: Correct. These are the three architecture components, and this chapter focuses on the client connector part.

choices.text: File reputation, file sandboxing, and file retrospection
choices.why: These are the three Malware Defense features, not its architecture components.
These are management objects inside the console, not the architecture components.
These are the three Secure Endpoint engines, not the three architecture components.

questions.q: Although the cloud makes most decisions, which protective action does the chapter say the Secure Endpoint connector can also take on its own?

choices.text: Sandbox unknown files on the endpoint
choices.why: File sandboxing is a cloud-based analysis of unknown files, not something the lightweight connector does locally.

choices.text: Block malicious network connections using custom IP blacklists
choices.why: Correct. The connector can act on its own, for example blocking malicious network connections using custom IP blacklists or dynamic lists of malicious IPs.

choices.text: Return Clean, Malware, or Unknown verdicts locally for any file
choices.why: Verdicts come from the Malware Analytics Cloud; the connector sends hashes there rather than deciding all files locally.
Cisco updates its maintained exclusions in the cloud and pushes them to connectors; connectors do not update them on their own.

questions.q: Which four platforms are supported by Cisco Secure Endpoint connectors?

choices.why: ChromeOS is not one of the four connector platforms; the fourth is Android.
Correct. Secure Endpoint runs on Windows, Mac, Linux, and Android endpoints.
iOS devices appear through iOS Clarity via a linked MDM; the fourth connector platform is Linux.
Solaris is not a connector platform, and Mac is missing; the four are Windows, Mac, Linux, and Android.

questions.q: Put the steps for creating a simple custom detection in the correct order.

choices.text: Create IP List, enter SHA-256 hashes one per line, then click Create IP List
choices.why: Create IP List is for DFC IP allow and block lists, which hold IPv4 addresses, not file hashes.

choices.text: Open Management > Exclusions, choose an OS, then add a SHA-256
choices.why: Management > Exclusions creates exclusion sets, which stop scanning; it is not where simple custom detections are built.

choices.text: Add a SHA-256, click Build Database From Signature Set, then name the detection
choices.why: Build Database From Signature Set belongs to advanced custom detections, and the detection is named before hashes are added.

choices.text: Open Custom Detections > Simple, enter a name and Save, add a SHA-256 or upload a file, then click Save
choices.why: Correct. You open the Simple list, name it with Update Name and Save, add a hash or file with a note, and click Save so the hash is stored.

questions.q: In a simple custom detection, an administrator selects a file and clicks a button so the cloud calculates its SHA-256. Which button is it?

choices.why: Correct. Upload sends the file so the cloud calculates its SHA-256, and the hash appears at the bottom right.
Download retrieves an IP list's file so you can change it; it does not hash an uploaded file.
View Changes opens the audit log for a list; it does not compute hashes.
Edit opens a list's contents on the right side; it does not compute a file's hash.

questions.q: An administrator added the wrong SHA-256 to a simple custom detection. Which console action deletes that hash from the list?

choices.why: Correct. Remove deletes an unwanted SHA-256 from the list.
This shows Cisco's exclusion sets and does nothing to a custom detection's hashes.
Create starts a new application blocking list; it does not delete a hash.
Update Name names or renames the detection; it does not delete hashes.

questions.q: An auditor asks who changed a particular simple custom detection and when. Which console link shows this?

choices.why: This compiles an advanced custom detection; it does not show change history.
Files included shows the hashes and notes currently in the detection, not the history of changes.
Management > Download Connector gets connector installers, not audit history.
Correct. Every simple and advanced custom detection has a View Changes link that opens its audit log.

questions.q: A user renames a blocked application's executable to bypass Secure Endpoint application control. Why does the block still work?

choices.text: Application control identifies applications by SHA-256 hash, not by name
choices.why: Correct. Applications are detected, blocked, and allowed by SHA-256 hash, so a new filename does not change the match.

choices.text: DFC detects the renamed file's IP address
choices.why: DFC works on network connections, not file names or hashes.

choices.text: Application control blocks every executable by default
choices.why: Application control only acts on the hashes in its lists; it does not block every executable.

choices.text: The Ethos engine checks the file's name pattern
choices.why: Ethos is a fuzzy fingerprinting engine; the reason the block holds is that application control uses SHA-256 hashes.

questions.q: A company wants to stop employees from installing an approved-but-unwanted game on corporate Android phones. Which use of Android custom detections fits?

choices.text: An IP block list for the game's servers
choices.why: IP block lists drive DFC network detections; they do not identify or remove Android apps.
Advanced custom detections target Windows and Mac files; Android detections are defined separately.

choices.text: A Windows path exclusion with CSIDL
choices.why: CSIDL path exclusions apply to Windows files and stop scanning; they do not remove Android apps.

choices.text: Application control, which notifies the user and prompts uninstall
choices.why: Correct. On Android, application control uses custom detections to stop unwanted apps, prompting the user to uninstall as with malicious apps.

questions.q: Cisco updates one of its Cisco-maintained exclusion sets. What happens to the policies that use it?

choices.text: Each administrator must approve the update for each policy
choices.why: No manual approval is described; the policies using the set update automatically.

choices.text: The policies keep the old version until the connector is reinstalled
choices.why: The update is pushed to connectors; no reinstall is needed.

choices.text: The exclusion set is converted to a custom detection
choices.why: Exclusions and custom detections are different objects; an update does not convert one into the other.

choices.text: Every policy using it updates and the change is pushed to connectors
choices.why: Correct. When a Cisco-maintained exclusion is updated, every policy using it updates too and connectors receive the change.

questions.q: By which attributes can an administrator search exclusion sets in the Secure Endpoint console?

choices.text: Group heat map or severity only
choices.why: The heat map and severity sorting are Inbox filters, not the exclusion set search fields.

choices.text: IP address, port, or CIDR range only
choices.why: IP addresses, ports, and CIDR ranges are IP list entries, not exclusion set search fields.
Trajectories are visibility features for files and endpoints, not exclusion search criteria.

choices.text: Name, path, extension, threat name, or SHA-256
choices.why: Correct. Exclusion sets can be searched by name, path, extension, threat name, or SHA-256, and filtered by OS with tabs.

questions.q: When clicking New Exclusion Set under Management > Exclusions, what must the administrator choose?

choices.why: These are cloud verdicts, not options when creating an exclusion set.
Simple and Advanced are custom detection types under Outbreak Control, not exclusion set choices.
Correct. A new exclusion set starts by choosing Windows, Mac, or Linux.

choices.text: IP Allow List or IP Block List
choices.why: That choice is made when creating an IP list under Outbreak Control > Network.

questions.q: An organization has Windows laptops and Linux servers and wants different connector behavior for each. How does Secure Endpoint support this?

choices.text: Only Outbreak Control lists can differ, not policies
choices.why: Policies combine Outbreak Control lists, exclusion sets, and other settings, and they are configured per platform.

choices.text: A different policy can be configured for each platform
choices.why: Correct. Policies are configured per platform, so Windows and Linux can have different policies, applied through groups.

choices.text: Linux servers must use Cisco Secure Client instead
choices.why: Linux is a supported Secure Endpoint connector platform with its own policy; Cisco Secure Client is a VPN and posture client.

choices.text: One policy is shared by all platforms and cannot differ
choices.why: The chapter says you can configure a different policy for each platform.

questions.q: Which filters can be applied to the Secure Endpoint Main Dashboard?

choices.why: Exclusion types are threat, extension, wildcard, and path; they are not dashboard filters.
Signature types belong to advanced custom detections, not to Main Dashboard filtering.

choices.text: Platform, date range, and other attributes
choices.why: Correct. The Main Dashboard can be filtered by platform, date range, and other attributes.
IPv4 addresses and ports are IP list entries for DFC, not Main Dashboard filters.

questions.q: An analyst repeatedly filters the Inbox to the same group and wants that view every time the Inbox opens. What can be done?

choices.text: Mark the group's computers as resolved
choices.why: Resolving computers removes them from Dashboard and Inbox data, which is the opposite of what the analyst wants.

choices.text: Create an exclusion set for the group
choices.why: An exclusion set stops the connector from scanning items; it does not change the Inbox view.

choices.text: Save the filter and set it as the default view
choices.why: Correct. Inbox filters can be saved and set as your default view.

choices.text: Enable iOS Clarity for the group
choices.why: iOS Clarity is a dashboard for MDM-managed iOS devices; it does not save Inbox filters.

questions.q: The iOS Clarity dashboard lists devices that have not reported back in more than how long?

choices.why: The iOS Clarity threshold is more than seven days, not 90.
The threshold is more than seven days, not 24 hours.
Correct. iOS Clarity lists devices that have not reported back in more than seven days.
30 days is the period the Main Dashboard shows; the iOS Clarity threshold is seven days.

questions.q: On a Cisco Email Security Appliance (ESA), what does a listener do?

choices.text: Flags suspicious network flows on endpoints
choices.why: Flagging suspicious network activity on endpoints is device flow correlation in Secure Endpoint.

choices.text: Handles incoming SMTP connection requests on an interface
choices.why: Correct. An ESA listener handles incoming SMTP connections and marks the edge of the email-processing service on an interface.

choices.text: Monitors jailbreak detection on mobile devices
choices.why: Jailbreak detection is an MDM monitoring function, not an ESA listener.

choices.text: Sends file hashes to the Malware Analytics Cloud
choices.why: Sending hashes to the cloud is what the Secure Endpoint connector does, not an ESA listener.

questions.q: What is mobile device management (MDM) defined as in the chapter?

choices.text: Centrally configuring, updating, monitoring, and remotely troubleshooting mobile and user devices
choices.why: Correct. MDM centrally configures, updates, monitors, and remotely troubleshoots phones, tablets, laptops, and other user equipment.

choices.text: Recording endpoint events in a central database for threat hunting
choices.why: That describes EDR, which focuses on detecting and investigating suspicious activity.

choices.text: Correlating device network flows with malicious IP lists
choices.why: That is device flow correlation (DFC) in Secure Endpoint.

choices.text: Analyzing unknown files to observe their true behavior
choices.why: That is file sandboxing, a Malware Defense feature.

questions.q: Why is known malware detected quickly by Cisco Secure Endpoint while the connector stays lightweight?

choices.text: Each connector stores a full local signature database
choices.why: A full local signature database is the traditional antivirus model; Secure Endpoint sends hashes to the cloud instead.

choices.text: Cloud resources do the analysis instead of endpoint resources
choices.why: Correct. Known malware is detected fast because cloud resources do the work, so the connector stays lightweight.

choices.text: Exclusion sets skip scanning of all known files
choices.why: Exclusion sets skip specific directories, extensions, or threat names; they are not how known malware is detected.

choices.text: The TETRA engine is enabled by default on every connector
choices.why: TETRA is disabled by default, and enabling it makes the connector thicker, not lighter.

questions.q: Which Malware Defense feature continues analyzing files over time as threat levels change?

choices.why: File reputation analyzes files inline to block them or apply policies at the time they are seen.
Correct. File retrospection keeps analyzing files as threat levels change.
Application control detects, blocks, and allows applications by SHA-256 hash; it is not ongoing file analysis.
Device trajectory shows what actions files performed on a given endpoint; it is not ongoing analysis of the file.

questions.q: Figure 11-1 shows the Malware Analytics Cloud working with which Cisco group, which the notes identify as Cisco's threat intelligence group?

choices.why: Cisco Meraki SM is an MDM that feeds iOS Clarity, not the threat intelligence group in the architecture figure.
Cisco Umbrella is one of the products integrated with Cisco Threat Response, not the threat intelligence group.
Correct. Talos appears with the Malware Analytics Cloud in Figure 11-1 and is Cisco's threat intelligence group.
SourceFire was the company whose FireAMP product became Secure Endpoint; it is not the threat intelligence group.

questions.q: The firewall form of Cisco Secure Malware Defense, covered in Chapter 7, is called Cisco Secure Firewall Malware Defense. What was its former name?

choices.why: FireAMP was the SourceFire endpoint product that became Secure Endpoint, not the firewall form.
Threat Grid was the former name of Cisco Secure Malware Analytics, the sandboxing product.
AMP for Endpoints was the former name of Cisco Secure Endpoint, the endpoint connector.
Correct. Cisco Secure Firewall Malware Defense was formerly AMP for Networks.

questions.q: Where do modern EDR solutions take in threat intelligence from, according to the chapter?

choices.why: Exclusion sets list items not to scan; they are not threat intelligence.

choices.text: Only from manually imported signature files
choices.why: Modern EDR relies on cloud threat intelligence, not only manual signature imports.
The ESA listener handles incoming SMTP connections; it is not the threat intelligence source for EDR.
Correct. The chapter says modern EDR solutions take in threat intelligence from the cloud.

questions.q: Besides improving performance, what is the other main use the chapter gives for Secure Endpoint exclusion sets?

choices.text: Distributing the connector to remote users
choices.why: Connector distribution uses installers, download URLs, or the AMP Enabler, not exclusion sets.

choices.text: Resolving conflicts with other security products
choices.why: Correct. Exclusion sets resolve conflicts with other security products and fix performance problems.
Quarantining files by hash is the job of custom detections, which are the opposite of exclusions.
Blocking IP addresses is done by DFC with IP block lists, not by exclusion sets.

questions.q: What two things does the connector do differently for items covered by an exclusion set?

choices.text: It quarantines them and notifies the user
choices.why: Quarantining and notifying is what custom detections do, not exclusions.

choices.text: It will not scan them and will not convict them as malware
choices.why: Correct. An exclusion set lists directories, extensions, or threat names the connector won't scan and won't convict.

choices.text: It blocks their network traffic and logs it in DFC
choices.why: Blocking network traffic is a DFC function; exclusions only affect scanning and conviction.

choices.text: It sends them to sandboxing and to retrospection
choices.why: Excluded items are skipped, not sent for extra analysis.

questions.q: An engineer needs to exclude all files ending in a certain pattern across several folders, such as temporary files with varying names. Which exclusion type fits best?

choices.why: Correct. Wildcard exclusions use wildcards in filenames, extensions, or paths.
A threat exclusion excludes by threat name, not by filename or path pattern.
A path exclusion covers files in one given path; it does not match patterns across varying names and folders.
An extension exclusion matches a file extension exactly, without wildcard patterns in names or paths.

questions.q: A known false positive is repeatedly convicted under the same detection name. Which exclusion type excludes items by the name of the detection?

choices.why: An extension exclusion excludes by file extension, not by threat name.
A wildcard exclusion uses wildcards in filenames, extensions, or paths, not threat names.
A path exclusion excludes files in a given path, not by threat name.
Correct. A threat exclusion excludes by threat name.

questions.q: Which navigation path is used to start a new application blocking list in Secure Endpoint?

choices.text: Outbreak Control > Application Control > Blocked Applications, then Create
choices.why: Correct. Application blocking lists are created from Outbreak Control > Application Control > Blocked Applications with Create.
This path creates advanced custom detections based on ClamAV signatures, not application blocking lists.
Management > Groups creates groups of computers for policies, not application blocking lists.

choices.text: Outbreak Control > Network > IP Block & Allow Lists
choices.why: This path creates DFC IP lists, not application blocking lists.

questions.q: When adding applications to a Secure Endpoint application blocking list by uploading files, how many applications can be uploaded at a time for the console to hash?

choices.text: Up to ten at a time, each within 100MB
choices.why: The chapter says one application at a time with a 20MB limit.

choices.text: Only Android .apk files may be uploaded
choices.why: Application blocking lists accept application files for hashing; .apk uploads are for Android custom detections.

choices.text: One at a time, each within the 20MB limit
choices.why: Correct. You upload one application at a time, up to 20MB, for the console to hash; you can also upload an existing list.

choices.text: Any number, with no size limit
choices.why: There is a 20MB limit, and uploads for hashing are one application at a time.

questions.q: An administrator needs to download the Secure Endpoint installer for the Engineering group or copy its download URL. Which console location is used?

choices.why: Correct. After picking a group, Management > Download Connector lets you download installers or copy their URL.
iOS Clarity shows MDM-managed iOS device activity; it does not provide connector installers.
Management > Exclusions lists and creates exclusion sets, not connector installers.
This path manages simple custom detections, not installers.

questions.q: A company has many remote workers who rarely connect to the corporate network. Which connector distribution method from the chapter helps them most?

choices.text: Create an IP allow list for their home addresses
choices.why: IP allow lists tell DFC which addresses never to block; they do not distribute the connector.

choices.text: Add the users to a Cisco-maintained exclusion set
choices.why: Exclusion sets control scanning; they do not install connectors.

choices.text: Email the download URL so users install the connector themselves
choices.why: Correct. Emailing the download URL lets users install it themselves, which the chapter says helps remote workers.

choices.text: Save the installer on an internal network share
choices.why: A network share is a valid method, but remote workers who rarely connect would struggle to reach it.

questions.q: When adding a signature to a Secure Endpoint advanced custom detection, how is the signature type determined?

choices.text: It can be auto-detected or picked from a drop-down list
choices.why: Correct. The signature type can be auto-detected or chosen from the drop-down list, as in Figure 11-6.

choices.text: It is inherited from the group's policy
choices.why: The type is chosen or auto-detected when adding the signature, not inherited from a policy.

choices.text: It is always fixed to SHA-256
choices.why: SHA-256-only lists are simple custom detections; advanced detections support more signature types.

choices.text: It is set by the Ethos engine
choices.why: Ethos is a fuzzy fingerprinting engine; it does not choose signature types in the console.

questions.q: An administrator pasted a SHA-256 into a simple custom detection and added a note, then navigated away. Later, the hash is missing. What most likely happened?

choices.why: TETRA is a client-side antivirus engine; it does not edit console lists.

choices.text: Simple custom detections only accept MD5 hashes
choices.why: Simple custom detections use SHA-256 hashes; MD5 is a signature type in advanced detections.

choices.text: The hash was moved to a Cisco-maintained exclusion set
choices.why: Hashes are not moved into Cisco-maintained exclusions; those are Cisco-created compatibility sets.

choices.text: The administrator did not click Save, so the hash was not stored
choices.why: Correct. The chapter warns that a hash isn't kept until you click Save.

questions.q: Which of these can be used to filter the Secure Endpoint Inbox?

choices.why: IP allow lists are DFC objects; they are not Inbox filters.

choices.text: Selecting a SHA-256 from the Significant Compromise Artifacts list
choices.why: Correct. The Inbox can be filtered by heat map groups, a day in the bar chart, a Significant Compromise Artifacts SHA-256, or a Compromise Event Types entry.
CSIDL names are used in Windows path exclusions, not Inbox filters.
Logical signatures belong to advanced custom detections, not Inbox filtering.

questions.q: Which Secure Endpoint view shows compromised computers and tracks compromises that need manual work to resolve, sortable by date or severity?

choices.why: The Events dashboard shows the most recent events in the deployment, not a work queue of compromises.
The audit log shows change history for lists and exclusion sets, not compromised computers.
iOS Clarity covers MDM-managed iOS devices and apps, not the compromise work queue.
Correct. The Inbox shows compromised computers, tracks those needing manual resolution, and can sort by date or severity.

questions.q: What does a Secure Endpoint policy combine to control the connector's behavior?

choices.text: Only Inbox filters and dashboard views
choices.why: Inbox filters and dashboards are reporting views, not policy contents.

choices.text: Only the connector installer and its download URL
choices.why: Installers and URLs are obtained from Management > Download Connector; a policy controls behavior through lists and settings.

choices.text: Outbreak Control lists, exclusion sets, and other settings
choices.why: Correct. A policy combines Outbreak Control lists, exclusion sets, and other settings and is configured per platform.
MDM profiles belong to tools like Meraki SM; Secure Endpoint policies combine Outbreak Control lists, exclusions, and settings.

questions.q: Which statement about Spero best describes how it judges software?

choices.text: By exact matches against a local signature database
choices.why: Exact local signature matching describes traditional antivirus such as TETRA, not Spero.

choices.text: By fuzzy fingerprints from static heuristics
choices.why: Fuzzy fingerprinting with static or passive heuristics describes Ethos, not Spero.

choices.text: By its general appearance using generic models, rather than specific patterns or signatures
choices.why: Correct. Spero builds generic models from execution attributes and judges software by its general appearance.

choices.text: By the IPv4 addresses the software connects to
choices.why: Judging connections by IP address is device flow correlation, not Spero.

questions.q: The chapter calls automated update and patch provisioning by MDM its main point on endpoint patching strategy. What benefit does it give?

choices.text: Keeps devices consistent and patches security vulnerabilities effectively
choices.why: Correct. Automated update and patch provisioning keeps devices consistent and patches security vulnerabilities effectively.

choices.text: Replaces the need for any EDR agent
choices.why: Patch provisioning keeps devices updated; it does not provide the detection and response that an EDR agent does.

choices.text: Turns on the TETRA engine automatically
choices.why: TETRA is a Secure Endpoint policy setting, disabled by default, and unrelated to MDM patching.

choices.text: Lets the connector skip cloud lookups
choices.why: Patch provisioning does not change how the connector gets verdicts from the cloud.
